segments.text: Hey friends, do you know someone who wants to eliminate bad
habits from their life, but those habits just won’t go away?
They’ve become addicted—and addiction isn’t limited to alcohol or drugs.
It could be an addiction to scrolling on the mobile phone, lying around
all day, being lazy, or eating junk food.
These are some
of the bad habits that have entered their life and just aren’t leaving.
And it’s not that he isn’t trying.
He has tried many times, made repeated efforts to get rid of these
bad habits, but every time he tried, he failed.
Maybe something like this is happening with you as well.
If yes, then please watch today’s video till the end.
This is going to be one of my best videos for you, where I’m
going to share not one, not two, but five powerful Japanese philosophies.
When combined, these philosophies create a system—and this system can eliminate
even the worst and dirtiest habits.
Each of these philosophies
is so powerful that you’ll find an entire book written on each one.
But today, I’m going to explain in a systematic way how you can
apply these five philosophies in your life.
I’ll also share how I personally created my channel based on these philosophies,
and how everything I’ve achieved and wherever I am today is because of them.
The five Japanese philosophies
we’ll talk about today are Kaizen, Ikigai, Hara Hachi Bu, Ganbaru, and Wabi-Sabi.
I’ll explain all these philosophies
through a story, but please, please, please watch this story till the end.
This is going to be one of the best stories on this channel
because the lessons inside it are truly very practical and useful—and
they have the power to make the coming year the best year of your life.
They have the power to eliminate any bad habit you have.
So once again, I’ll say this—please watch
the video till the end, because I’m not going to explain this in theory.
I won’t just entertain you in a story format; by the end of this video,
I’ll also show you how you can practically apply these ideas, and how I
can personally help you implement them in your life—at a very
minimal cost, which you’ll find out about at the end of the video.
So please, please, please watch the video till the end.
Now let’s start.
David, a 40-year-old man, had collapsed on his knees in his neighbor’s garden.
Sweat was dripping onto the ground, his breathing was extremely heavy, and
his nine-year-old son was silently watching him.
He was drowning in shame—so much so that he couldn’t even speak.
Just then, the neighbor came and helped him up, and that night he cried a lot.
Why did he cry?
Well, here’s the thing—David was a 40-year-old man
whose weight had reached 140 kilos, and he was slowly dying.
At least, that’s what the reports showed: his cholesterol levels had gone extremely
high, he had developed
type-2 diabetes, and all his blood reports were in very bad condition.
The doctors had given him an ultimate warning: take care
of your health, or you’ll face serious problems in the future.
Now look—he wasn’t a bad person at all.
He was kind-hearted, a very good human being, and hardworking.
He was a shop manager and had been doing the same job for 15 years.
Every day he would wake up in the morning, work hard till evening,
and then go home. He had two children.
He had a wife.
He had bills to pay.
Basically, he was a typical middle-class man who had become so entangled in the
web of responsibilities
that he completely forgot he also had a body that needed care.
His diet was whatever he could get, whenever he could get it.
Breakfast while traveling, lunch was whatever he could grab from here or there.
Dinner was eaten while watching TV, because he was so exhausted from morning
till night that
he didn’t even have the energy to talk—just eat while watching something.
Weekends meant full-on partying: pizza, beer, the sofa.
After all,
a person deserves at least this much if he works so hard all week, right?
These things did give him pleasure, but now, more than pleasure,
they were starting to feel like a punishment.
His body had started giving him signals, but he kept ignoring them.
Even if he walked a little, he would start gasping for breath.
Bending down to tie his shoelaces felt like solving a puzzle—figuring out
how to bend, where to place his hands, and how to manage it somehow.
Even just sitting down, he often had to stop and catch his breath.
He had to press his stomach to get comfortable.
Sometimes his wife would
say, “Let’s go for a walk,” but he simply didn’t have the strength to go.
If the kids asked him to play, he didn’t have the energy for that either.
It wasn’t his weight that made him feel the most ashamed—it was
the fact that his seven-year-old daughter had stopped even asking, “Come on,
Papa, let’s play,” because she had already understood that Papa would never play.
He simply didn’t have the strength, and all of this was making him feel terrible.
It wasn’t that David had never tried.
He joined three different gyms at different
times and even hired trainers, but after a month or two, he would quit.
He also started a low-carb diet, but even that he gave up within three weeks.
He started running in the mornings, but gave that up too within three or four
days.
And while doing all this, he had reached a dangerous place—where people are
alive, but somewhere inside them, something dies.
They start accepting it: “This is just how life will be now.
This is how I am. My body is meant to be fat.
My genetics are fat.” “I don’t have time.” But then came one evening
when he was with his children while they were playing.
He was somehow adjusting himself on a plastic chair, sitting and watching
them play.
Suddenly, one of the kids’ balls went into the neighbor’s garden.
Since he had already told them not to go there, the child requested, “Daddy,
will you please go and get my ball?” Somehow,
he managed to pull himself up from the chair and slowly started walking.
He began to run out of breath, and the moment he bent down
to pick up the ball, he realized that he couldn’t control his balance.
Both his hands and knees ended up on the ground.
It wasn’t that he was injured or that something very serious had happened.
No, it was a simple thing—his legs no longer had the strength
to lift his own body.
And his little child was watching all of this.
Sweat dripping, gasping for
breath, when the neighbor helped David up, tears came to his eyes.
Not because he had fallen or was in pain.
He cried.
Because his child had
seen him in that condition—a condition no father would want his child to see.
A weak, defeated father.
He felt like a loser.
That day, he went home and cried a lot.
Then his wife comforted him, hugged him, and said, “That’s enough.
Now you have to do something about this.” That day, David started thinking
about what he should do next.
And then he remembered a friend of his—a friend who wasn’t exactly
like him, but who was also very overweight and had successfully lost 30–40 kilos.
He was the only friend who had completely transformed
and maintained his transformation, so David went to him for guidance.
When David
met Jacob, he asked him, “What method did you follow?
What are you eating?
What treatment are you doing that allowed you to transform yourself
so well?” Then Jacob told him, “Look, I don’t have any magical treatment.
But yes, there is a doctor.
I went to him, and this doctor is not an ordinary doctor.”
This doctor doesn’t give medicines.
This doctor changes your mindset
and teaches philosophies to transform your life.
Now, David didn’t understand much of this at first, but still,
since he had to try, he went to see the doctor.
When he arrived at the doctor’s house, he saw books everywhere—books
stacked all around—and it didn’t feel like this was a normal doctor.
David went to him and told the doctor his whole story—how his weight had been
steadily increasing, his
fatigue, the embarrassment in front of his children—he shared every detail.
When he finished, he was expecting that this doctor would give him a new
diet plan, a magical exercise routine, or ask him to do some blood tests.
Just like many others had said before.
But the doctor said something David wasn’t expecting.
The doctor asked him, “David, tell me one thing—how much time have you actually
given yourself to change?” He couldn’t even remember—two months, five months?
Then the doctor said, “Do you know why you failed?
Because of your genetics being weak, or your timetable
not being right?” Well, the doctor said, “No, you failed because the amount
of time you gave to become your worst self, you haven’t even given half of that.
You aren’t even giving 10% of that time to become your best version.
The amount of time you are giving to create your best version isn’t
even 10% of the time you’ve spent creating your worst version.” Don’t you think
this is unfair?
You’ve lived your lifestyle one way for
40 years, and you expect that in two or five months you can
completely change yourself?
Now, David didn’t fully understand
all of this, but still he said, “Doctor, what should I do?
Please tell me.” Then the doctor said, “I’m going to give you a challenge.”
The challenge will be so small that you might think it’s a joke.
But remember, it’s not a joke.
If you really want to change, this is what you’ll have to do.
David said, “Doctor, whatever you say,
I will do it.” The doctor said, “Starting tomorrow morning, after you wake
up, you have to drink a glass of water.” David didn’t say anything at that moment.
He was expecting the doctor to give him more instructions, but the
doctor said, “That’s it.” This shocked David a lot—just drink a glass of water.
In the morning, just for two weeks, drink it and nothing else.
The doctor said, “No, eat pizza,
drink beer—live your lifestyle exactly as you have been for these two weeks.”
You just have to do one thing—drink a glass of water every morning.
Now, after hearing this, David got a little frustrated.
He said, “Doctor, I need to lose at least 50 kilos—what will a glass of water do?”
Then the doctor told him, “I will tell you what this glass of water
will do only after you come back having done this for two weeks.”
And if you’re serious, you will definitely do this.
We won’t talk about anything beyond this right now.
We’ll discuss it after two weeks.
David asked the doctor to promise him that he would drink water for two weeks
every morning.
Somehow, David agreed to the promise, but he was very angry.
He felt, “Hey, I paid ₹5,000 for this consultation!”
He thought, “I’ve been ruined—this seems like a scam.” But still, he kept
his promise and that night placed a glass of water next to his bed.
The next morning, he drank it immediately after waking up.
Day one, day two, day three—because
he had promised and needed to meet the doctor again, he started doing it.
His weight hadn’t reduced at all yet, but slowly, something began to change.
By the fourth, fifth, and seventh day, when there wasn’t a glass of water next
to his bed in the morning, he felt a little strange and immediately
went to fill a glass and drink it.
By the second week, drinking water had become somewhat
of a habit for him, and if he didn’t drink it, he felt a little off.
After this, two weeks later, he went to the doctor and said, “Doctor, I did
exactly as you told me.” “But my weight hasn’t reduced at all—what are you even
making me do?” Then the doctor said, “My goal was never to make you lose weight.
What we needed to achieve was something that you have now successfully done.
That one thing was keeping a promise.
How many times have you promised yourself that you’ll go to the gym today, do this,
do that—and how many times have you broken those promises?” Think
about it—you probably can’t even count how many times you’ve broken promises.
But this time, you made a promise to yourself, a promise to me,
that you would get up every morning and drink water—and you did it.
You kept your promise, and this is the first step toward a
drastic transformation.
And this is where the first Japanese
philosophy comes in: Kaizen—improving one percent daily.
Many times, to change our lives, we feel that we need to do very big things.
But if you do even a small task—just one percent—that can make you
better, you won’t see results immediately.
But one day, the results will definitely show.
David analyzed this a little and said, “Doing this really made me feel a
bit silly.
And to be honest, I’ve even lost one kilo.” But one kilo is nothing.
The doctor smiled
and told him, “You have successfully completed your first Japanese philosophy.
The first challenge is complete.” Kaizen is about small changes and
continuous improvement.
Many times, to climb a whole mountain, you don’t need to climb it all
at once—just keep taking one step, and eventually, the mountain will be climbed.
But the story doesn’t stop here.
You have now developed a keystone habit.
This will become your base.
The concept of a keystone habit, taken from the book The Power of Habit,
is a habit that, once established in your life, triggers other good habits.
Often, that one keystone habit is enough to change your entire life.
Drinking water every morning will be that keystone habit that you need to do daily.
But the story doesn’t stop here.
In the first step, by taking
this small step, you have proven to yourself that change is possible.
Now, in the next step, you will take yourself a little higher.
And again, we have to do this using Kaizen—improving by one percent.
If you improve yourself daily, it won’t just be 365%—you will have grown
exponentially, around 3,778%.
Now, the next step is this: for the next three weeks, whatever
you eat, eat only half the portion.
And if you still feel hungry after that, you can
eat more—but at least wait for the first 20 minutes.
If you feel hungry after 20 minutes, then eat; if not, don’t eat.
Now, this wasn’t very easy for David either, but he said, “Okay, I’ll do it.”
He started following this, and even here, something amazing began to happen.
In the beginning, he felt a little discomfort eating
less, but this thought kept running in his mind.
I can wait 20 minutes and then eat.” But when he actually started waiting
those 20 minutes, he realized that after 20 minutes,
he didn’t feel like eating as much anymore.
And this is the Japanese philosophy
he came to understand, called Hara Hachi Bu—eat until you are 80% full.
The doctor
hadn’t explicitly explained it to him, but he experienced Hara Hachi Bu firsthand.
Basically, it means
that our brain needs time to realize whether our stomach is full or not.
Many times, when we eat too
quickly, the brain doesn’t get enough time to process whether the stomach is full.
That’s why we often overeat, which later leads to stomach pain and other problems.
But when you eat half your portion and give
yourself 20 minutes, the food has time to properly reach your stomach and
send the signal: “Yes, I am full.” David was surprised when he did this.
Only 3–4 times did he go back for more food, while the
rest of the time he stuck to eating just half his portion.
Because of doing this, he lost three kilos.
Now, three kilos out of 140 wasn’t a very big deal.
And when he went to the doctor and told him that this had happened—that
in three weeks he had lost only three kilos—the doctor said, “It’s not about
the weight; it’s about the direction.
For the first time in your life, you are moving in the right direction.
For the first time, the control of your life is coming into your hands.”
David agreed on this—yes, maybe his weight hadn’t reduced that much.
But for the first time, he felt that, yes, he could change
his life and that the control of his life was in his hands.
After this, for
the third task, the doctor gave him a challenge to add movement into his life.
And what does adding movement mean?
He didn’t say, “You have to go to the gym and spend a lot of time there.” No.
He asked David, “Is there any physical
activity you can normally do?”—but so far he had been avoiding it.
After thinking
for a bit, David realized, “Yes, I can go from my house to the mailbox
where the letters are kept.” He said, “I can add that movement into my life.”
But he said, “That’s very little.
My mailbox is just 20, 30, 40 meters from my house—how is that going to be
exercise?” Again, the doctor said, “Your body has forgotten the habit of movement.
Right now, we just need to remind your body that it was
made for movement, and that’s why starting this task daily isn’t too much.”
Just go to the mailbox and come back—go to the mailbox and come back.
When David started doing this, it didn’t feel very significant to him.
But a few days later, he realized that his little seven-year-old daughter had
started watching daily how her dad goes
to the mailbox, stops there, checks the mail, and then comes back.
And because his daughter loved talking to her dad—a thing she often wanted
to do but couldn’t—she said, “Dad, I want to walk with you too.” Every day,
they would go to the mailbox together, talking along the way, collect the
mail, and come back.
Gradually, David and his daughter enjoyed talking and spending time so much that
they automatically started walking
a little farther, up to the corner of the street.
While talking to each other, they started doing three things together for a
month: drinking water every
morning, eating half portions, and walking—which became a half-hour walk.
Because of this, he lost eight kilos in a month.
David started feeling a little excited.
He went to the doctor and happily shared how he now talks with his daughter
while walking, and their relationship and bonding were getting stronger.
Then the doctor asked him, “David, why are you doing all this?
Is it just to lose weight?” David was confused.
He said, “I want to lose weight because I’m overweight.” The doctor
said, “No, think carefully—what is the actual reason you want to lose weight?
What is your exact reason?” And when David thought about it, he realized that what
he truly wanted from his
heart was to be strong enough to stand for his family members.
When his daughter grows up, he wants to give her a grand wedding.
He wants to play with his child for a long time and be their support.
Then the doctor said, “This is where the third Japanese philosophy comes in:
Ikigai—the reason for doing what you are doing.
Losing weight alone won’t be enough motivation.
Until you attach it to a higher purpose, your Ikigai isn’t just losing weight.”
Your Ikigai is to be available for your family in an energetic
mode—so that you can give time and energy to your children, play with them,
give loving time to your wife, and overall enjoy life with your family.
Because look, if you only focus on losing weight, the motivation will come and go.
But now, when you attach a
purpose behind everything you do, it will become a fuel that never runs out.
Some days, you might not feel like drinking water or going for a walk.
But every time
you remember your purpose—that you need to move, that you need to lose weight
so you can watch your children grow and be there for your grandchildren—it will
keep you going.
Being healthy will help you stand strong even in difficult times.
As they were talking about this, David’s eyes filled with tears.
He told the doctor, “You are right, and I will definitely keep this purpose close
to my heart.” After this, David continued doing the same things—nothing
extraordinary, just these habits.
But then suddenly, one day, the doctor received a call from David.
He sounded panicked and said, “Doctor, I messed up.
I have ruined everything.
I’ve destroyed it all.
Everything has gone wrong—I’ve
failed again.” The doctor asked calmly, “What happened?” Then David explained
that there was a wedding in his relatives’ family, and he had gone to attend it.
He tried to eat only half his portion, but the people there insisted, “Eat, it’s
nothing, just one day.” Under that peer pressure, he ended
up eating a lot of food, and afterward, he felt extremely guilty.
He felt like all his progress had been completely ruined.
Then the doctor called him over and asked him to recount the entire incident again.
David explained how he felt that everything was ruined, that
he would regain all the weight and would never get slim again.
Then the doctor asked him a simple question.
He asked, “David, tell me—did you drink water this morning?” David said, “Yes.”
Then he asked, “After waking up today, did you eat only half your portion again?”
He said, “Yes.” The doctor asked, “Did you go for your walk today?”
He said, “Yes.” Smiling, the doctor said, “This doesn’t mean you have failed.
It just means your steps faltered, and now you’re ready to keep walking
again.” Then the doctor told him about the fourth Japanese principle, Wabi-Sabi.
Wabi-Sabi is basically a Japanese philosophy that celebrates imperfection
and teaches that nothing in life is permanent or perfectly flawless.
Nothing is ever complete, but it is these imperfect things that hold true beauty.
The doctor explained to him that one day’s mistake cannot erase months of progress.
It does not nullify your daily habit of drinking water in the morning,
nor does it erase the time you spent with your daughter each day.
The 14 kilos you have already lost will not come back because of one mistake.
Hearing this,
something inside David broke—what broke was his expectation tied to perfection.
Earlier, he thought that if he was going to do something,
he had to do everything perfectly; otherwise, it wasn’t worth doing.
Many times, he had failed
because he couldn’t run or do things as perfectly as he had imagined.
He couldn’t go to the gym as effectively as he had planned.
But the doctor explained to him that perfectionism is a huge enemy
of consistency.
However, if you stay consistent, even
if you are imperfect, it will still take you to your goals.
David told the doctor that he had made such a mistake again, and the doctor
explained, “David, you will make mistakes again, and probably many times.”
But at that time, you need to remember one thing: come back to your keystone habit.
No matter what goes wrong, keep focusing on drinking water
every morning, going for your walk, and eating only half your portion.
Every time you stumble, come back to these habits.
This is where the fifth Japanese philosophy, Ganbaru, comes in—never
giving up during the toughest times and continuing to persist.
Keep going so that your consistency doesn’t break.
After hearing this, David felt much lighter somewhere inside.
Instead of scolding him, the doctor explained, “It’s okay—things will happen
here and there, it doesn’t matter.” This gave David more courage to say, “Alright,
it’s okay.” After that, he started again, and he didn’t have to start from zero.
He had already lost many kilos.
He just had to keep going and
not think of any excuses to quit, which the doctor had explained to him.
And what was the result?
In six months, David lost 23 kilos.
People started to be amazed
at the change, but the real transformation wasn’t just on the weight scale.
David truly felt the real transformation
when he was playing with his son and his toy fell to the ground.
Without any effort, David picked up the toy—his breath wasn’t even heavy.
When his wife watched this from a distance, a smile appeared on her face,
and that smile was because, in a way, her husband had truly come back.
That old laughter, that familiar face, that old essence of her husband—which had
been lost somewhere—had returned.
Many good days came, and many bad days came.
But David never let go of his keystone habit.
He kept at it, stayed consistent.
The result: in one year, he lost 35 kilos.
Now everyone started asking him, “What are you doing?” “How are
all these changes happening?” he asked his friends.
He told them, “No, nothing special, just making small changes here and there.”
Later, when he went to the doctor, the doctor asked David a
very important question.
He asked, “David, tell me—when was the last time you felt like giving up and
never doing something again?”
“Now I don’t want to drink water, I don’t want to walk, I don’t want to eat half
my portion.” David paused
for a moment and thought—last week, last month… but to be honest, David said,
“I don’t even remember.” The doctor said, “Do you know why this is happening?
It’s because now you’re not trying to change yourself—you have already
changed.” Your
identity has changed, because over the past year you have repeated these habits
so many times that they have become a part of you—they have become your identity.
You are no longer an overweight person.
You are someone who is losing weight, taking care of yourself, caring for
your children, and transforming.
Time passed like this.
In one and a half years, he lost 52 kilos.
His goal was to get below 100 kilos, and he achieved it.
When David looked at himself in the mirror afterward, he still
wasn’t the healthiest person in the world—he didn’t have six-pack abs.
But now, looking in the mirror, he felt proud of himself.
Where earlier he felt ashamed looking at himself, now he
felt like a warrior—even seeing his loose skin didn’t bother him.
And he achieved this one step at a time.
Later, when
he went for another blood test and the reports came back, everyone was shocked.
Even the doctor he had been visiting was amazed seeing him.
The doctor asked, “What treatment are you following that has completely normalized
your cholesterol,
reversed your diabetes, and improved all the indicators that were previously bad?
What magic pill are you taking that brought such a
change?” David smiled and replied, “Nothing, I just drink a glass
of water every morning.” The doctor didn’t get the joke, but for David,
this joke was very powerful—a keystone habit that had changed his entire life.
Later, when David happily went to his doctor to share the good news about how
much his health had improved,
the doctor told him, “Remember, your entire transformation wasn’t magic.”
These were just 5 core concepts that we applied one by one.
Systematically, your transformation started
with focusing on Kaizen—one percent improvement.
You began simply by drinking water, creating a keystone habit that became
your foundation for transformation.
Then you applied Hara Hachi Bu, which means eating less than what you feel you
need, not more.
Instead of overdoing anything, you kept everything balanced.
Third, you discovered your IKIGAI, your purpose.
Fourth, you understood wabi-sabi—accepting imperfection.
And fifth, Ganbaru—you didn’t give up, gave your best, and
stayed persistent even in the most difficult times.
And this five-step system is not just for weight loss.
If you apply this
anywhere in your life, you will definitely get results—100 percent.
David’s transformation wasn’t
life-changing just for him; it was for his children too.
Seeing David, they were inspired.
They realized, “I can also do tough work.
I can also be disciplined.” His wife gained the courage to improve herself.
By taking on this challenge, David didn’t just change his own life—he transformed
his entire family’s life and taught lessons
that his children and future generations would remember and be inspired by.
Friends, if you also want to change something in your life or eliminate bad
habits, you need to apply these five philosophies and mindset
principles in your life.
